skyline.text: Charles Booth’s study, be­fore the dis­ci­plines went their own ways
How a non-specialist picks up the rhythm of pa­pers
Heraclitus, and why two snap­shots miss how change hap­pens

brief.head: Increasing returns
brief.text: The more you know, the more new knowl­edge sticks, Ajay Shah said: “the learn­ing process has in­creas­ing re­turns to scale”. So read, even if you for­get. {075-C02}

brief.head: Stock and flow
brief.text: Amit Varma bor­rows two eco­nom­ics terms for cre­ators. Flow is tweets, col­umns and episodes; stock is last­ing work, like Milton Friedman’s *Free to Choose*. The best pa­pers are both. {075-C04}

brief.head: Not every village
brief.text: Internal va­lid­ity asks if your claims hold for the vil­lage you stud­ied, Ajay Shah said; ex­ter­nal va­lid­ity asks if they hold else­where. Keep the two apart. {075-C14}

brief.head: Philosophers, Pvt Ltd
brief.text: Ajay Shah wants the word philoso­pher back for any­one eclec­tic. Plato and Aristotle stud­ied ev­ery­thing, Amit Varma had said, and every label cuts a sub­ject off. {075-C16}

brief.head: Uphill to breadth
brief.text: Formal knowl­edge pro­duc­tion has over­done spe­cial­i­sa­tion, Ajay Shah said, so al­most ev­ery­one would gain from more breadth: “there is a nice lovely gra­di­ent to be climbed”. {075-C17}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: Our loy­alty should be to ques­tions.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, against economics’ lurches from one methodological fad to the next

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on a paper by Biju Rao
lead.head: Numbers, with the tears put back

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 75

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah set out to dis­cuss two pa­pers they both love. Time went by, lunch called, and they got through one. {075-J08}

The one they did dis­cuss was Vijayendra Rao’s *Can Economics Become More Reflexive?* It ar­gues that eco­nom­ics, an­thro­pol­ogy and so­ci­ol­ogy, once part of the same quest to un­der­stand so­ci­ety, drifted into silos and stopped learn­ing from one an­other.
Its cen­tral thought, Varma said, is the show’s own: ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing.
Rao, a World Bank econ­o­mist known to his friends as Biju, has a line Varma loves: “The meth­ods lead the ques­tions, rather than the other way around.” {075-C05}
Once a field is loyal to one method, it can ask only the ques­tions that method can an­swer. Incentives then lock the method in place.
## Four lessons from the field
Rao sets out four things econ­o­mists can learn from ethno­g­ra­phers, and Varma took them in turn.
The first is cog­ni­tive em­pa­thy, Mario Small’s phrase: not imag­in­ing your­self in someone’s shoes, but “see­ing an­other per­son as they see them­selves”.
The sec­ond is to take words se­ri­ously. “Numbers don’t tell you the full story,” Varma said. “Words can tell you a lot.”
The third is process. Two snap­shots of a place miss how change ac­tu­ally hap­pens; the ethno­g­ra­pher stays on the ground and watches it un­fold.
The fourth is par­tic­i­pa­tion. The very word “sub­jects”, Varma said, im­plies dis­tance. Ethnographers make the peo­ple they study par­tic­i­pants in­stead.

Rao learnt the first les­son in the field. In a vil­lage in 1992, women talk­ing to his team blamed the state for their trou­bles for about a week, until trust was built and they spoke of beat­ings at home. {075-S04}
## Clubhouses and fads
Why did the dis­ci­plines split? Universities set up de­part­ments, Shah said, and pro­mo­tion came to de­pend on pub­lish­ing in each discipline’s own jour­nals.

In eco­nom­ics, he said, one fad after an­other wins the jour­nals and, through them, the ap­point­ments. There was a time for ran­domised con­trol tri­als, for in­stru­men­tal vari­ables, for ex­per­i­men­tal eco­nom­ics. Scholars must con­form or leave. Insisting on method­olog­i­cal pu­rity, he said, is “very child­ish”.
## Close, but not too close

Shah was can­did about his own lean­ings. He loves India, he said, and wor­ries that root­ing for it bends his judge­ment, so he takes refuge in data. He quoted a line he finds beau­ti­ful: “sta­tis­tics are human be­ings with the tears washed away”. {#tears}
Varma’s an­swer was to go nearer: “you gotta get closer to that and see the tears, but not cry your­self.” {075-C13}

Shah, for his part, has al­ways talked to peo­ple out­side his for­mal re­search: prac­ti­tion­ers in Bombay, of­fi­cials, politi­cians, any­one with a fac­tory to show. “Go out of your room and bloody talk to the peo­ple,” he said.

The episode had begun with a ques­tion about read­ing. Shah’s ad­vice came from the econ­o­mist Ed Glaeser: “read books for ideas, read pa­pers for tech­niques.” Papers, he said, have chased rigour so hard that “the very pur­suit for rigor has in­duced rigor mor­tis”.
Rao’s paper, Varma said, shows no sign of it.

second.label: How to read a book
second.head: Seeing like a reader
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the book he argued with on almost every page

pic.caption: James C. Scott in 2016
pic.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

body: One of the wildest read­ing ex­pe­ri­ences of Ajay Shah’s life was James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*. On al­most every page, he said, he was ar­gu­ing with the au­thor. {075-S02}

Sometimes he dis­agreed. Sometimes he was un­happy, be­cause Scott was going some­where “com­pletely an­ti­thetic” to what he then thought. Sometimes he of­fered other ex­pla­na­tions. The book is not per­fect, he said; it sim­ply came when he was “primed and ready for it”. {075-R08}

He reads every paper the same way, as an ar­gu­ment with the au­thor, rather than with the rote mem­ory of Indian exams. Amit Varma’s ver­dict: Scott had cured him of “the fatal dis­ease of see­ing like an en­gi­neer”. {075-J02}

quote.text: I just re­mem­ber lit­er­ally page after page my mind would be burst­ing with the con­ver­sa­tion.

third.head: The title gives it away
body: When a paper stud­ies Tamil Nadu but leaves Tamil Nadu out of its title, Ajay Shah said, be more scep­ti­cal of the work. “This is a guy grab­bing for fame and glory.” {075-C18}
It is a dis­ease of the ad­vanced economies, he said, where pa­pers on America do not put America in the title, though the work is about one nar­row lo­cale and the re­sults do not gen­er­alise.
Shah said he does not share the ar­ro­gance of econ­o­mists who be­lieve they are cre­at­ing uni­ver­sal truth. Every lo­cale is dif­fer­ent.
A mod­est title and a mod­est ab­stract, he said, speak well for the human qual­i­ties of an au­thor. The oth­ers are “just like frat boys run­ning for ten­ure”. {075-J07}

p2.title: Out of the silos
p2.deck: Vijayendra Rao’s paper on what economists can learn from ethnographers, read by Amit Varma and argued over with Ajay Shah

from1.head: Numbers, with the tears put back

quote.text: If you look at the meth­ods be­hind this, you couldn’t say that this is eco­nom­ics, or this is an­thro­pol­ogy, or this is so­ci­ol­ogy.

box.title: The paper behind the episode
box.text: Vijayendra Rao’s *Can Economics Become More Reflexive?* traces how eco­nom­ics, an­thro­pol­ogy and so­ci­ol­ogy split apart, and of­fers econ­o­mists four lessons from ethnog­ra­phy: cog­ni­tive em­pa­thy, words, process and par­tic­i­pa­tion. Amit Varma said it could be a book by it­self. {075-R01}

sections.label: The divergence
sections.head: The venue sets the tune
sections.caption: three disciplines drifting apart
body: Economics, an­thro­pol­ogy and so­ci­ol­ogy were once part of the same quest, Amit Varma said: to un­der­stand so­ci­ety, and why human be­ings be­have the way they do. Through the 20th cen­tury, driven by in­cen­tives, each re­treated into its own lane: quan­ti­ta­tive eco­nom­ics, cul­tural an­thro­pol­ogy, qual­i­ta­tive so­ci­ol­ogy. {075-C05}

Vijayendra Rao’s paper opens with a work from be­fore the split: Charles Booth’s study of the peo­ple of London, com­piled in the late 19th cen­tury over, Varma thought, some 17 years. It used data, house­hold sur­veys, in­ter­views and ob­ser­va­tion, and cov­ered em­ploy­ment, ill­ness, fam­ily size and habits like thrift. {075-S03}

Then the meth­ods began to lead the ques­tions. Varma re­called the show’s episode on cre­ativ­ity, where the venue shaped the music: per­cus­sion in the open air, none in the echo­ing gothic churches of Europe. {075-R21}
## Scale or depth
The econ­o­mist, Varma said, stays de­tached, works through sur­vey agen­cies and gets scale. “You can­not do a weather re­port of, say, Karjat by only fo­cus­ing on Karjat,” he said. {075-C06}

The ethno­g­ra­pher em­beds in one com­mu­nity and gets nu­ance, but may miss the for­est for the trees. The an­thro­pol­o­gist Bhrigupati Singh, quoted by Rao, de­scribes mov­ing from hunter-gatherer to set­tled cul­ti­va­tor, “from im­pres­sions to ex­pres­sions”.
~ Michael Burawoy, in *The Extended Case Method*, held that the pos­i­tivist and the re­flex­ive ap­proaches are nec­es­sar­ily sep­a­rate. Rao ar­gues they need not be. {075-R04}

quote.text: If you look at the meth­ods be­hind this, you couldn’t say that this is eco­nom­ics, or this is an­thro­pol­ogy, or this is so­ci­ol­ogy.

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Not your shoes, their eyes
sections.caption: cognitive empathy
body: The first thing econ­o­mists can learn from ethno­g­ra­phers, in Vijayendra Rao’s ac­count, is cog­ni­tive em­pa­thy, a phrase coined by Mario Small. {075-C08}

“Cognitive em­pa­thy is see­ing an­other per­son as they see them­selves,” Amit Varma said. If you see some­one as poor and starv­ing, your mir­ror neu­rons may kick in as you imag­ine their hunger. But how that per­son sees them­selves could be rad­i­cally dif­fer­ent.
## A week to the truth

Rao learnt this in a vil­lage in 1992, where women spent a week blam­ing the state be­fore trust let them speak of vi­o­lence at home. Without that field­work, Rao wrote, they would never have thought of study­ing do­mes­tic vi­o­lence. {075-S04}

The les­son, Varma said, is not to send a sur­vey group, get some num­bers and then “give gyan from a dis­tance”. Talk to peo­ple, he said, stay with them for a while, and try to get a deeper in­sight into what is going on.
~ Varma noted the re­flex­iv­ity too. When a hus­band dragged his wife from the room for talk­ing to Rao, the re­searcher saw that his pres­ence had changed the sit­u­a­tion.

quote.text: But it is to ac­tu­ally un­der­stand from that per­son how do they see them­selves.

sections.label: Lessons two to four
sections.head: Words, rivers and stones
sections.caption: words, process and participation
body: The sec­ond les­son is to take words se­ri­ously. Economists take num­bers se­ri­ously, Amit Varma said, but the nar­ra­tives peo­ple tell about them­selves, fol­lowed over time, give a far bet­ter pic­ture than num­bers alone. {075-C09}

It must be done rig­or­ously, not by draw­ing large con­clu­sions from a few quotes. Varma ex­pects ma­chine learn­ing to help sift through, say, ten thou­sand in­ter­views from vil­lages, where hu­mans tend to see what they are pre­dis­posed to see. {#ml}
## Feeling the stones

The third les­son is process. Since the cred­i­bil­ity rev­o­lu­tion, Rao writes, em­pir­i­cal eco­nom­ics has been al­most en­tirely fo­cused on mea­sur­ing out­comes. Two snap­shots, Varma said, miss change as it hap­pens. {075-C10}
No man steps in the same river twice, he said, re­call­ing Heraclitus: the man has changed, and the river has changed. {075-J11}
Then, for Ajay Shah’s ben­e­fit, he quoted “your favourite Chinese per­son­al­ity”, Deng Xiaoping, on cross­ing the river by feel­ing the stones. {075-J12}

The fourth les­son is par­tic­i­pa­tion. In 2014, Rao and a World Bank team asked tribal com­mu­ni­ties in South Indian vil­lages what mat­tered to them, and built their ques­tion­naire from the an­swers. It shared only 17 per cent of its ques­tions with the National Sample Survey.
~ That sur­vey, Varma sug­gested, was pos­si­bly de­signed in Delhi by some bu­reau­crats.

quote.text: What is not done is often to do the most ob­vi­ous thing, to keep a close eye on the ground
quote.who: Vijayendra Rao, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The incentives
sections.head: Fads at the clubhouse door
sections.caption: journals, fads and context
body: Once, Ajay Shah said, there were thinkers about the world called philoso­phers, and no dis­ci­plinary bound­aries. Then uni­ver­si­ties set up de­part­ments, and hir­ing, fir­ing and pro­mo­tion cre­ated “tremen­dous in­cen­tive dis­tor­tions in each field”. {#departments}
Senior pro­fes­sors told schol­ars to prove them­selves in a few jour­nals, each “the lit­tle club­house of that dis­ci­pline”, and the vi­sion nar­rowed. {#clubhouse}

In eco­nom­ics, Shah said, a fad wins, takes the jour­nals and through them con­trols ap­point­ments. Every aca­demic must then exit or con­form. Diverse views often go un­pub­lished, and the peo­ple who de­cide, he added, re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else.
## Not the in­ter­ven­tion alone

Data has its own blind spot. Reading a paper that cred­ited e-filing in one coun­try with cer­tain re­sults, Shah ob­jected that some 500 sub­tle de­tails of law, pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion, in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture, cul­ture and norms were at work. {#fivehundred}
“It’s not the in­ter­ven­tion that did it,” he said, “it is the in­ter­ven­tion in all that con­text.” {075-C15}
~ His rem­edy is old-fashioned: panel data, ob­serv­ing the same firms and house­holds across the coun­try over and over, to make av­er­age claims about India.

quote.text: re­al­is­ti­cally we are all peo­ple and peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives and the peo­ple who con­trol jour­nals re­spond to in­cen­tives

sections.label: Learn the thumri
sections.head: Every paper is a thumri
sections.caption: how to read a paper
body: How should a reader spend their time? Entering a new sub­ject, Ajay Shah said, first get the big pic­ture through broad read­ing that in­te­grates knowl­edge, and only then dive into nar­row tech­ni­cal pa­pers. {#bigpicture}
After dozens of episodes of *Everything is Everything*, he said, he and Amit Varma have a co­her­ent view of field after field, so they are en­ti­tled to read one nar­row paper at a time.
## Getting the rhythm

Shah’s first port of call for any search is Google Scholar, not Google. Even if you can­not fol­low a paper’s tech­ni­cal in­nards, he said, “in time you will get the rhythm, you will get the feel”. {075-R14}

The en­gine of a paper is IMRD: in­tro­duc­tion, method­ol­ogy, re­sults, dis­cus­sion. Read the ab­stract and in­tro­duc­tion, get a sense of the method­ol­ogy, skim the re­sults and read the dis­cus­sion. {075-C19} It is part of his recipe, he said, for read­ing pa­pers in a very large num­ber of dis­ci­plines.

~ The hosts closed with rec­om­men­da­tions. Varma chose EH Gombrich’s *The Story of Art*, which, he said, is also the story of think­ing and of sto­ries; Shah chose Kenneth Clark’s *Civilisation*. {075-R11}

quote.text: It is a thumri and it is an art form, and you’ll get fa­mil­iar with what is a thumri
Our tears shouldn’t get into the pic­ture, but we have to see their tears, un­der­stand why those tears are there, where they come from, what do they think about it.

p3.title: Tales from the field
p3.deck: A village, a city, a confession and a mall, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Biju Rao’s fieldwork in 1992, as told by Amit Varma
stories.head: Trust first, then the truth
body: In 1992, the World Bank econ­o­mist Vijayendra Rao, known as Biju, was with a group of re­searchers in a vil­lage, talk­ing to women about their house­hold in­come and their lives. {075-S04}
In a room full of women, a hus­band walked in, grabbed one of them by the hair and pulled her out. Her sin, Amit Varma said, was talk­ing to Rao.
Rao re­alised that by putting him­self in the sit­u­a­tion, he was chang­ing it. That, Varma said, is re­flex­iv­ity.
For about a week, the women blamed the state. The schools were ter­ri­ble, they said, and there was no good drink­ing water. {#week}

Then, once trust was built, one of them told Rao: “You have be­come our friends and we can’t lie to you any­more. Let me tell you the truth. We feel like we are in jail. Our hus­bands beat us all the time and no one helps when that hap­pens.”

Tracked over time, the qual­i­ta­tive and quan­ti­ta­tive data linked the vi­o­lence to power within the fam­ily, to fe­male ster­il­i­sa­tion, which raised the risk of being ac­cused of in­fi­delity, to al­co­holism and to dowry de­mands. The vi­o­lence, Rao wrote, was often a ra­tio­nal choice to ex­tract money from the wife’s fam­ily.

~ No eco­nom­ics jour­nal would pub­lish the mixed-methods ver­sion. It came out years later as two pa­pers, one in a pub­lic health jour­nal and one in an eco­nom­ics jour­nal. “This is just com­pletely point­less,” Varma said.
stories.why: Detached sur­veys would have missed the story en­tirely: with­out the field­work, Rao wrote, they would never have thought of study­ing do­mes­tic vi­o­lence. And jour­nal in­cen­tives split one rich study into two par­tial ones.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the women who stopped lying

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a study that belonged to every discipline
stories.head: The book no department can claim
body: In the late 19th cen­tury, Charles Booth set out to por­tray the peo­ple of London. The work took, Amit Varma thought, about 17 years, and filled a whole bunch of vol­umes. {075-S03}
It used data, house­hold sur­veys, par­tic­i­pant in­ter­views and plain ob­ser­va­tion. {075-R03} And it was not done once: it was a con­tin­u­ous process over those years.

It cov­ered em­ploy­ment, which is easy to ask about, but also cir­cum­stances that are harder to ar­rive at, such as ill­ness, in­fir­mity and fam­ily size, and habits: who drank, and how thrifty peo­ple were.
~ The re­sult, Varma said, was a mag­is­te­rial pic­ture of London, its rich and its poor and how its neigh­bour­hoods were evolv­ing. For Vijayendra Rao, such work was part of a dying breed.
stories.why: Before the dis­ci­plines split, so­cial in­quiry used every method it could find. Twentieth-century in­cen­tives, in Rao’s ac­count as Varma told it, pushed that kind of work aside, and the meth­ods began to lead the ques­tions. {075-C05}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Charles Booth’s London

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the trouble with rooting for India
stories.head: If only it were Cambodia
body: Ajay Shah wor­ries about him­self. “I care so much about India that I feel it in­ter­feres with my ob­jec­tiv­ity,” he said. “Like, I’m root­ing for us and that is a prob­lem.” {075-S06}
If he stud­ied Cambodia, he said, he would be a good scholar; study­ing India is dan­ger­ous. {#cambodia} Amit Varma as­sured him that he was still a good scholar.

The mind is a slip­pery thing, Shah said. Loyalty to tra­di­tional Indian cul­ture, re­spect for one’s fore­fa­thers or sim­ply want­ing India to suc­ceed can slide into pro­pa­ganda and nar­ra­tive bat­tles that make him feel good. Cultural pride, he said, is dam­ag­ing for ob­jec­tiv­ity.
~ And when he goes close to the ex­pe­ri­ence of mass de­pri­va­tion in India, the blood rushes to his head. “I run away,” he said. “I take refuge in data.”
stories.why: Honest schol­ar­ship treats one’s own at­tach­ments as bi­ases to guard against, and choos­ing data can be self-knowledge rather than cold­ness. Varma’s reply was to see the tears, but not cry your­self. {075-C13}
stories.postscript: Later, Shah added that he and Susan know they can­not stay re­mote: “That’s one of the rea­sons why we hide in the data.” {#susan}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on rooting for India

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the research he never writes up
stories.head: Four hours in a mall
body: Ajay Shah never brings peo­ple into his for­mal re­search. Papers, he said, are “for­mal set piece bat­tles”. But he has de­signed his life around talk­ing to the peo­ple in the econ­omy. {075-S07}

One of the best places in India to study the Indian econ­omy, he be­lieves, is Bombay: it holds fi­nan­cial and non-financial firms, and ev­ery­day con­ver­sa­tions with prac­ti­tion­ers are rich with in­sights.

It takes many years of trust, he said, be­fore peo­ple stop giv­ing you their press re­leases. He talks to of­fi­cials and politi­cians. Once, a firm’s head of mar­ket­ing walked him through a mall for four hours, ex­plain­ing the busi­ness. {#mall}

~ What peo­ple say about their rea­sons, though, is not nec­es­sar­ily the ex­pla­na­tion. As Milton Friedman taught, Shah said, the bil­liards player never says he thought about Newton’s laws, yet be­haves as if he did.
stories.why: Conversations on the ground bring com­mon sense and hy­pothe­ses, Shah said; then you turn around and do the clean data work. What peo­ple tell you is the truth as they know it, which need not be the truth.

quiz.q: Which line from the economist Ed Glaeser did Ajay Shah offer on what to read?
quiz.a: “Read books for ideas, read pa­pers for tech­niques”: big ideas now live in books.

quiz.q: What is cognitive empathy, in the phrase Vijayendra Rao borrows from Mario Small?
quiz.a: Seeing an­other per­son as they see them­selves, not as you see them.

quiz.q: How much of the tribal communities’ 2014 questionnaire overlapped with the National Sample Survey?
quiz.a: Only 17 per cent of its ques­tions were in com­mon with the sur­vey.

quiz.q: Why did Biju Rao’s research on domestic violence appear as two separate papers?
quiz.a: No eco­nom­ics jour­nal would pub­lish the mixed-methods ver­sion, so it was split in two.

quiz.q: What makes Ajay Shah sceptical of a paper that studies Tamil Nadu?
quiz.a: A title with­out Tamil Nadu in it: the au­thor is grab­bing for fame.

quiz.q: What art form did Shah compare a research paper to, and why?
quiz.a: A thumri: with ex­po­sure, you pick up its rhythm even with­out tech­ni­cal train­ing.

glossary.def: An art form whose rhythm, Shah said, comes with ex­po­sure
Knowledge or ad­vice, often handed out from a lofty dis­tance
Research in which ob­servers en­gage, know­ing they change what they ob­serve
Detached re­search using stan­dard­ised data and rep­re­sen­ta­tive sam­ples
Repeated ob­ser­va­tions of the same firms or house­holds over time
Whether find­ings from one vil­lage hold else­where, or na­tion­wide

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 75. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Charles Booth (George Frederic Watts, public domain); Deng Xiaoping (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Ernst Gombrich (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Kenneth Clark (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain).

shelf.title: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
shelf.creator: Vijayendra Rao
shelf.why: Vijayendra Rao’s ar­gu­ment, which is the show’s own the­sis that ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing, that eco­nom­ics has drifted into a silo away from an­thro­pol­ogy and so­ci­ol­ogy, with four things econ­o­mists can learn from ethno­g­ra­phers: cog­ni­tive em­pa­thy, tak­ing words se­ri­ously, study­ing process and mak­ing peo­ple par­tic­i­pants.

shelf.title: Biju Rao Won’t Bow to Conventional Wisdom (Episode 392 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite episodes: Biju Rao ar­gues that you can’t make pol­icy from data on a desk in Washington but have to get your hands dirty on the ground, and that India has its own deep tra­di­tion of vil­lage-level de­lib­er­a­tive democ­racy.

shelf.title: Life and labour of the people in London
shelf.creator: Charles Booth
shelf.why: A 17-year, multi-volume study that mixed sur­veys, in­ter­views and ob­ser­va­tion so freely that you can’t as­sign it to any one dis­ci­pline.

shelf.title: The Extended Case Method
shelf.creator: Michael Burawoy
shelf.why: It con­trasts the pos­i­tivist ap­proach (de­tach­ment, stan­dard­ised data, rep­re­sen­ta­tive sam­ples) with the re­flex­ive one (en­gage­ment, em­bed­ding your­self in a com­mu­nity).

shelf.title: Narrative Economics
shelf.creator: Robert Shiller
shelf.why: Amit’s ex­am­ple of the grow­ing recog­ni­tion that num­bers don’t tell the full story and that the nar­ra­tives peo­ple hold mat­ter.

shelf.title: Terror as a Bargaining Instrument: A Case Study of Dowry Violence in Rural India
shelf.creator: Francis Bloch & Vijayendra Rao
shelf.why: The re­search found do­mes­tic vi­o­lence was often a ra­tio­nal strat­egy to ex­tract money from the wife’s fam­ily, which pushed econ­o­mists to re­think how they model house­hold and trans­fer be­hav­iour.

shelf.title: Domestic Violence and Intra-Household Resource Allocation in Rural India: An Exercise in Participatory Econometrics
shelf.creator: Vijayendra Rao
shelf.why: It shows what com­bin­ing qual­i­ta­tive and quan­ti­ta­tive work re­veals: links be­tween vi­o­lence and fam­ily power, ster­il­i­sa­tion, al­co­holism and dowry.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Free to Choose (1980 and 1990 series)
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: An ac­ces­si­ble, watch­able ver­sion of Friedman’s case for free­dom, and Amit’s ex­am­ple of last­ing work that be­comes a body of knowl­edge oth­ers build on, un­like the daily flow of tweets and col­umns.

shelf.title: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case for read­ing: ex­pe­ri­ence gives us only a few dots, slowly, while books let us col­lect many dots fast, live many lives and reach deep, com­plex truths about the world that ex­pe­ri­ence alone can’t.

shelf.title: The Story of Art
shelf.creator: EH Gombrich
shelf.why: Gombrich ex­plains the con­text and sto­ries be­hind works of art, paint­ing by paint­ing, so even peo­ple who re­spond to art only vis­cer­ally can un­der­stand it.

shelf.title: Civilisation
shelf.creator: Kenneth Clark
shelf.why: A foun­da­tional book for him when he was young.

shelf.title: Seven Bridges Road
shelf.creator: Steve Young (original, 1969); The Eagles (live version, 1980)
shelf.why: He thinks both ver­sions are won­der­ful.

shelf.title: Google Scholar
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: It is his first stop for any search, ahead of Google.

shelf.title: Technology, Taxation, and Corruption: Evidence from the Introduction of Electronic Tax Filing
shelf.creator: Oyebola Okunogbe & Victor Pouliquen
shelf.why: A cau­tion­ary ex­am­ple rather than an en­dorse­ment.

shelf.title: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Dr Lancelot Pinto, one of the rare doc­tors who reads pa­pers daily, on med­i­cal prac­tice and how overtreat­ment driven by pa­tient de­mand cost lives dur­ing COVID.

shelf.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long de­fence of sci­en­tific medicine from liver doc­tor Abby Philips, on the ten­sion be­tween doing right by pa­tients and giv­ing them what they want.

shelf.title: Plato (or Why Philosophy Matters) (Episode 109 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is the source of his point that early philoso­phers were es­sen­tially sci­en­tists who in­quired into ev­ery­thing, be­fore sub­jects split off and got la­belled.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: How to Write a Paper (Episode 62)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ex­plains the IMRD struc­ture (Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion), which is the key to ex­tract­ing value from pa­pers out­side your field.

shelf.title: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How form shapes con­tent: the venue shapes the music, from per­cus­sion in the open air to none in echo­ing gothic churches to al­ter­na­tive rock in CBGB’s crowded room.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

laughs.text: After Ajay calls learn­ing ‘a bloody vi­cious cycle,’ Amit gen­tly cor­rects him: ‘At one point... you said vi­cious cycle. I would say vir­tu­ous cycle, which is surely what you meant.’
Amit, riff­ing on the title of Seeing Like a State: ‘James C. Scott cured you of the fatal dis­ease of see­ing like an en­gi­neer, which you no longer do.’
Ajay’s pun on aca­demic pa­pers: ‘the very pur­suit for rigor has in­duced rigor mor­tis.’
Ajay on what young aca­demics are told: ‘shut up and read pa­pers, shut up and write pa­pers, be nar­row, don’t think more, like just be a gal­ley slave like ev­ery­body else.’
Amit asks what to do about ‘too much breadth’ and, as Ajay pon­ders, pounces: ‘No no, you’re think­ing se­ri­ously, don’t think se­ri­ously. Ah, you’re think­ing of Ozempic.’
Ajay on au­thors who give nar­row stud­ies uni­ver­sal-sounding ti­tles: ‘they’re just like frat boys run­ning for ten­ure.’
Two pa­pers were promised, but only one was dis­cussed: ‘time has gone by, we have to go for lunch. We’ll talk about the other pa­pers some other time.’

Amit in­tro­duces Gombrich: ‘my rec­om­men­da­tion is noth­ing to do with the sub­ject of the episode, but ev­ery­thing to do with the sub­ject of this episode, be­cause ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing.’
Amit re­veals that Ajay has sung his own cover of Seven Bridges Road: ‘we’ll have to ne­go­ti­ate whether we can put a lit­tle bit of that video here. We’ll get a copy­right strike for fuck’s sake.’
Heraclitus’s ‘no man steps in the same river twice’ is Amit’s image for why snap­shots miss change: both the man and the river have changed.
Amit quotes ‘your fa­vorite Chinese per­son­al­ity,’ Deng Xiaoping, to Ajay: ‘cross­ing the river by feel­ing the stones,’ as the ethnographer’s way of fol­low­ing change step by step.

Milton Friedman’s bil­liards player, in­voked by Ajay: the player never says he thought about Newton’s laws, but be­haves as if he did. What prac­ti­tion­ers tell you about their rea­sons isn’t nec­es­sar­ily the real ex­pla­na­tion.

Amit on how venue shapes art: open-air set­tings suit per­cus­sion, the re­verb of gothic churches rules it out, and CBGB’s crowded room gave rise to al­ter­na­tive rock and funk. Methods shape re­search ques­tions the same way.
Amit on Plato and Aristotle as the orig­i­nal all-purpose in­quir­ers who stud­ied math, bi­ol­ogy and ethics alike, and his lament for the van­ished ‘Renaissance man.’
